title: New Year Chaos
directAnswer: People labeled 1..n start sorted. Anyone can bribe the person directly in front to swap, at most twice each. Given the final order, count total bribes. If any person's label is more than 2 positions ahead of where it started (`q[i] − (i+1) > 2`), print 'Too chaotic'. Otherwise the bribe count for person `q[i]` is the number of larger labels sitting in front of them — and you only need to scan from index `max(0, q[i]−2)` to make it O(n).

A bribe is counted from the **bribed** person's view: how many higher labels overtook them and now sit in front.
Start the inner scan at `max(0, q[i] − 2)`, not `0`. Anyone who passed `q[i]` moved forward ≤ 2, so they can't have started earlier than `q[i] − 2`.
Bribes can only move you **forward**; a person never moves backward voluntarily, which is why we count larger labels *ahead*, not behind.

remember.takeaway: The move cap of 2 turns a global inversion-count problem into a local one: each person can only be overtaken by neighbors who started within 2 positions, so a bounded window gives the count in O(n) instead of O(n²) or O(n log n).

interviewerIntent.testing: Whether you spot that the '≤ 2 bribes each' cap bounds how far the inversion can reach, letting you shrink an O(n²) scan to a windowed O(n) one — and whether you handle the 1-indexed label math without off-by-one errors.
interviewerIntent.commonMistake: Checking `q[i] − i > 2` (forgetting the +1 for 1-indexing) or scanning from index 0, which is correct but O(n²) and may TLE on large inputs.
interviewerIntent.toStandOut: Derive the chaos check from 'forward moves ≤ 2', then explain why the scan can start at `q[i] − 2`: anyone who bribed past person `q[i]` moved forward at most 2, so they couldn't have begun before `q[i] − 2`.

problemStatement:
Initially, people are standing in a queue numbered `1` to `n` in order. Any person can bribe the person directly in front of them to swap positions, but **each person can bribe at most twice**.

Given the final state of the queue `q`, determine the **minimum number of bribes** that took place to reach it. If anyone has bribed more than twice — detectable because their label has moved more than 2 positions forward — print `Too chaotic` instead.
constraints: Each person bribes at most twice when the state is valid
understanding: The queue is a permutation of 1..n. A label that ends up more than 2 spots ahead of its starting position is impossible under the 2-bribe rule → 'Too chaotic'. Otherwise, the minimum bribes equals the number of pairs that are out of order with a larger label in front — counted efficiently by only looking at the small window a person could have come from.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Are the labels 1-indexed?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Yes. Person q[i] started at position q[i] (1-based); their current 1-based position is i+1. The chaos check is q[i] − (i+1) > 2.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Whose bribe count am I adding — the briber's or the bribed person's?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: It's cleanest to count from the bribed person's perspective: every larger label now sitting in front of person q[i] represents one bribe that passed them.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Can a person move backward?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Only by being bribed past — they never initiate a backward move. That's why we only count larger labels ahead, never behind.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Why can I start the scan at q[i] − 2 instead of 0?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Anyone who overtook person q[i] bribed forward at most twice, so they couldn't have started earlier than q[i] − 2. Scanning before that wastes time.

approaches.complexityReasoning: For every index i you scan all j < i looking for larger labels — n(n−1)/2 comparisons, O(n²).
approaches.explanation:
A bribe is an adjacent swap that pushes a bigger label one step forward. So the total number of bribes equals the total number of *inversions* where a larger label sits in front of a smaller one — but with one twist from the rules.

**The chaos check comes first.** Person `q[i]` started at 1-based position `q[i]` and now sits at 1-based position `i + 1`. The forward distance travelled is `q[i] − (i + 1)`. Since each person can bribe at most twice, that distance can be at most 2. The instant any person exceeds it, the configuration is unreachable — print `Too chaotic` and stop. Note the direction: we only care about *forward* movement, because being pushed *backward* (a smaller `q[i]` than its index) is caused by others and is unlimited.

**Counting from the bribed person's side.** For person `q[i]`, every larger label `q[j]` with `j < i` is someone who overtook them — one bribe. Summing over all `i` counts each bribe exactly once: the bribe that moved a big label past a small one is attributed to the small (bribed) label. Counting from the briber's side double-counts and is fiddly.

**Why it's O(n²).** The naive count scans all earlier indices for each person. For `n = 10⁵` that's ~5 billion comparisons — too slow. The move cap is the lever to fix this.
approaches.insight: Counting bribes from the *bribed* person's perspective (larger labels in front) avoids the double-counting trap you fall into if you try to tally each briber's two moves directly.

approaches.name: Windowed Count — Greedy Bound (Optimal)
approaches.whenToMention: The answer they want for large n: scan only the window a person could have come from.
hints: If person q[i] was overtaken by someone, how far forward did that someone move? At most 2. So how early could the overtaker have started?
An overtaker of q[i] can't have a starting position earlier than q[i] − 2 — so don't scan before index max(0, q[i] − 2).
The inner scan now covers at most a constant-width window per person, so the whole pass is linear.
approaches.complexityReasoning: Each person's inner scan covers indices [max(0, q[i]−2), i). Because any overtaker moved forward ≤ 2, the window has bounded width, so total work across all persons is O(n).
approaches.explanation:
Same inversion count, but we exploit the move cap to shrink each person's scan to a tiny window.

**Why the window starts at q[i] − 2.** Suppose person `q[j]` (with `q[j] > q[i]`) is now in front of person `q[i]` — they overtook them. To get in front of `q[i]`, label `q[j]` had to move forward, and it can move forward at most 2. Label `q[j]`'s original position is `q[j] > q[i]`, so the furthest *back* an overtaker could have started is `q[i] − 1`… but using the safe, widely-accepted bound, anyone capable of sitting in front of `q[i]` started no earlier than position `q[i] − 2` (1-based), i.e. index `q[i] − 2 − 1` in 0-based — we use `max(0, q[i] − 2)` as the start of the scan to be safe. Scanning from index `0` would re-examine people who could never have overtaken `q[i]`.

**Why this stays correct.** We're not changing *what* we count — still 'larger labels in front of `q[i]`'. We're only skipping a prefix of indices guaranteed to hold no overtaker, because those people started too far back to legally reach in front of `q[i]` under the 2-move cap.

**Why it's O(n).** The chaos check already guarantees no one travels forward more than 2. That same cap bounds how many people can crowd in front of any given person to a small constant, so each inner scan is short and the whole algorithm is linear — fast enough for `n = 10⁵`.
approaches.insight: The constraint *is* the algorithm. 'Each person bribes at most twice' isn't flavor text — it's the bound that collapses a global O(n²) inversion count into a local windowed O(n) scan. Whenever a permutation problem caps per-element movement, look for a windowed count.

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Off-by-one in the chaos check
commonMistakesDetailed.why: q[i] is a 1-based label but i is a 0-based index. Comparing q[i] − i misjudges the forward distance by one and reports chaos too late or too early.

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Slow full scan on large input
commonMistakesDetailed.why: Scanning from index 0 for every person is O(n²); with n up to 10⁵ it times out. Start at max(0, q[i] − 2).

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Integer overflow on the accumulator
commonMistakesDetailed.why: Bribe totals can grow large across many inversions; an int can overflow in Java.

patternNote: Bounded inversion counting. A per-element movement cap converts a global O(n²)/O(n log n) inversion count into a local windowed O(n) scan. The chaos check is a greedy feasibility guard derived directly from the cap; the windowed count exploits the same cap.
